issues.issue: The installment schedule begins January 2, 2010 and runs to 2014 regardless of whether the LPT and settlement agreement are ever executed, while section IX provides that if those documents are not completed Lincoln General's remedy "shall be to refile the lawsuit." Whether the note payments survive a section IX failure is unaddressed.

The note must be "in a form substantially similar to Exhibit A," but no Exhibit A is attached to the executed Memorandum of Understanding. The referenced form is missing from the instrument, and "substantially similar" supplies no standard in its absence.

The parties' stipulation that the Memorandum is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement" cannot be squared with section IX, which limits Lincoln General's remedy for non-completion to refiling the lawsuit. Whether suit on the Memorandum or refiling the dismissed case is available must be construed between the two.

"[S]ufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement" is a recitation of a legal conclusion, and the provision does not say which obligations it is definite as to. Whether the parties can contract themselves out of indefiniteness as to sections I and X is left to construction.

"[T]olling and other litigation resumption agreements" names no form, no terms and no deadline, and "other litigation resumption agreements" has no defined content beyond the tolling example. It is an undertaking to execute unspecified future documents.

The tolling runs "for five (5) years of until all claims ... have been paid and settled," where the mangled conjunction leaves it unclear whether the period is five years, or until all claims are paid, or the longer or shorter of the two. "[P]aid and settled ... pursuant to any and all agreements between them" also fixes no ascertainable end date.

The provision incorporates the "Other Causes of Action" defined in "the April 28, 2008 letter agreement," but the letter agreement in the record is dated April 30, 2008. The misdescription puts in issue which document, and hence which definition, is being incorporated.

The April 2008 letter tolls the Other Causes of Action "until the Lawsuit has been settled or otherwise finally resolved, including the completion of any appeals," while section VI tolls them for five years or until all claims are paid. Which tolling term governs those causes of action after the Lawsuit's dismissal cannot be answered from either document alone.

Tolling is extended only to defenses, counterclaims and equitable theories the Defendants "are asserting in the Lawsuit at the time of its dismissal," which by its terms excludes theories not yet pleaded when the case was dismissed. What it means to "toll" a defense, as opposed to a claim, is also left unstated.

"[T]he same limitations posture as they had in the lawsuit prior to its dismissal" is an undefined phrase that does not say whether accrual, filing date, or relation-back is what is preserved. It must be read against the five-year toll in the same section to know which controls.

"[S]ubject to regulatory approval" identifies no regulator, no applicant, no deadline, and no consequence if approval is refused or never sought. Whether it is a condition precedent to the whole Memorandum or only to the LPT is unresolved on its face.

Making the Memorandum "and the matters to which it addresses" subject to regulatory approval cannot be squared with section V, under which the Memorandum is enforceable on execution and Lincoln General must immediately dismiss its case. Which provision fixes the moment of binding effect must be construed.

The heading covers "Failure to Complete the Required Actions ... or Later Breach," but the operative text addresses only the parties being "not able to complete" the contemplated documents and says nothing about breach. Whether refiling is also the remedy for a later breach, and whether it is an exclusive remedy at all, is left open.

Limiting Lincoln General's remedy to refiling the lawsuit cannot be squared with section V's agreement that the Memorandum is "sufficiently definite to allow the parties to sue for its enforcement," nor with the unconditional payment duty in section IV. A court must decide whether section IX displaces enforcement of the Memorandum.

The parties merely "agree to draft a settlement agreement" that will, "among other things," provide releases, leaving the releases' scope, parties, timing and remaining terms entirely for future negotiation. It is on its face an agreement to agree.

"[T]he particulars of the releases in Defendants' favor" and "that agreement's other terms" are wholly deferred to a document not yet drafted, so nothing in this provision fixes who is released or from what. The provision states an intention without any ascertainable content.

"[S]uch other and further documents and/or pleadings as may be reasonably necessary" sets no standard for what is reasonably necessary and no time for performance. Read with sections I and X it could be argued to compel execution of the LPT and settlement agreement whose terms are undetermined.
